```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
```


## Data load and preparation before modelling

```{r read_data}
gss16<-read.csv("data/gss16.csv")
```

#### Cleaning and selecting columns

```{r}
gss16_advfront <- gss16 %>%
  select(advfront, emailhr, educ, polviews, wrkstat) %>%
  drop_na()
```

#### Re-levelling `advfront`

```{r}
gss16_advfront <- gss16_advfront %>%
  mutate(
    advfront = case_when(
      advfront == "Strongly agree" ~ "Agree",
      advfront == "Agree" ~ "Agree",
      TRUE ~ "Not agree"
    ),
    advfront = fct_relevel(advfront, "Not agree", "Agree")
  )
```

#### Re-levelling `polviews`

```{r}
gss16_advfront <- gss16_advfront %>%
  mutate(
    polviews = case_when(
      str_detect(polviews, "[Cc]onservative") ~ "Conservative",
      str_detect(polviews, "[Ll]iberal") ~ "Liberal",
      TRUE ~ polviews
    ),
    polviews = fct_relevel(polviews, "Conservative", "Moderate", "Liberal")
  )
```


## Exercise 1: Create a linear regression model

#### Exercise 1 (a)

```{r linear-model-1}
email_mod_1 <- lm(emailhr ~ educ, data = gss16_advfront)
email_coef_1 <- tidy(email_mod_1, conf.int = TRUE)
knitr::kable(email_coef_1, digits = 4,
             caption = "Simple linear regression coefficients")
```

The fitted line is

\[
\widehat{\text{emailhr}} =
`r round(coef(email_mod_1)[[1]], 3)` +
`r round(coef(email_mod_1)[[2]], 3)`\,\text{educ}.
\]

Each additional year of education is associated with an estimated
**`r round(coef(email_mod_1)[[2]], 3)` additional hours spent on email per week**,
on average. The fitted value estimates mean weekly email hours for a given
education level; `emailhr` is the response, so there is no separate
`emailhr` regression coefficient. The intercept is
`r round(coef(email_mod_1)[[1]], 3)` hours at zero years of education.
This negative prediction is not physically meaningful and illustrates a
limitation of using a straight line for a non-negative response.

The analysis uses `r nrow(gss16_advfront)` complete observations from `r nrow(gss16)` original rows. These are observational, unweighted complete-case analyses; associations are not causal effects and cannot automatically be generalised to all US adults.

#### Exercise 1 (b)

```{r linear-model-1-fit}
email_glance_1 <- glance(email_mod_1)
# Display all columns returned by glance() in a readable vertical table.
email_glance_1 %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Statistic", values_to = "Value") %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 6, caption = "All model fit statistics from glance()")
```

The model has an R-squared of **`r round(email_glance_1$r.squared, 4)`**,
so education explains only **`r round(100 * email_glance_1$r.squared, 2)`%**
of the observed variation in weekly email hours. The adjusted R-squared is
`r round(email_glance_1$adj.r.squared, 4)`. The residual standard error is
`r round(email_glance_1$sigma, 2)` hours per week, indicating substantial
unexplained variation. The overall F-test gives
F(`r email_glance_1$df`, `r email_glance_1$df.residual`) =
`r round(email_glance_1$statistic, 2)` and
p = `r format(email_glance_1$p.value, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)`.
Thus there is evidence of an association, but statistical significance does
not imply useful predictive performance.

```{r scatterplot, fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Weekly email hours versus years of education, with the fitted regression line."}
ggplot(gss16_advfront, aes(x = educ, y = emailhr)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, colour = "#28536B") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = "#C05A32", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Years of education", y = "Email hours per week")
```

```{r linear-diagnostics, fig.width=8, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Residual diagnostics for the simple linear regression."}
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4.5, 5, 2, 2))
plot(email_mod_1, which = c(1, 2, 3, 5))
par(old_par)
```

The residual-versus-fitted plot shows a non-uniform vertical spread, with
large positive residuals at higher fitted values. The scale-location plot
also shows increasing residual spread, making constant error variance
questionable. The residual smoother trends down rather than remaining
horizontal around zero, which also raises doubts about the linear mean
relationship. The Q-Q plot departs strongly from the reference line in the
upper tail, indicating right-skewed, non-normal residuals and large outliers.
The residual-versus-leverage plot helps identify observations that could
influence the fitted line. The model also predicts negative hours at very
low education levels.

The plots do not establish that errors are independent; this depends on the
survey design, and respondents may be clustered. Overall, the low R-squared
and problematic residual distribution make this model weak for individual
predictions. Conventional standard errors and hypothesis tests should also
be interpreted cautiously because their assumptions are questionable.

## Exercise 2: Compare two linear models

#### Exercise 2 (a)

```{r linear-model-2}
email_mod_2 <- lm(emailhr ~ educ + advfront, data = gss16_advfront)
email_coef_2 <- tidy(email_mod_2, conf.int = TRUE)
knitr::kable(email_coef_2, digits = 4,
             caption = "Multiple linear regression coefficients")
```

"Not agree" is the reference category. Holding years of education constant,
respondents who agree with the statement are estimated to spend
**`r round(coef(email_mod_2)[["advfrontAgree"]], 3)` more hours per week on
email** than those who do not agree. Its 95% confidence interval is
[`r round(email_coef_2$conf.low[email_coef_2$term == "advfrontAgree"], 3)`,
`r round(email_coef_2$conf.high[email_coef_2$term == "advfrontAgree"], 3)`]
hours, and p =
`r round(email_coef_2$p.value[email_coef_2$term == "advfrontAgree"], 3)`.
This interval includes zero, so the data do not provide clear evidence of
an additional association after accounting for education. This is an
adjusted association, not a causal effect.

#### Exercise 2 (b)

```{r compare-linear-models}
email_glance_2 <- glance(email_mod_2)
linear_comparison <- bind_rows(
  "Education only" = email_glance_1,
  "Education + agreement" = email_glance_2,
  .id = "Model"
) %>%
  select(Model, nobs, r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma, AIC, BIC)

knitr::kable(linear_comparison, digits = 4,
             caption = "Linear models fitted to the same complete observations")
```

The new model explains **`r round(100 * email_glance_2$r.squared, 2)`%**
of the variation, with a residual standard error of
`r round(email_glance_2$sigma, 2)` hours. Both models therefore have poor
overall explanatory performance. Adding `advfront` increases ordinary
R-squared by only
`r round(100 * (email_glance_2$r.squared - email_glance_1$r.squared), 3)`
percentage points. Ordinary R-squared cannot decrease when a predictor is
added, so it is not sufficient evidence that the larger model is better.

**I prefer the education-only model:** it has the higher adjusted R-squared
(`r round(email_glance_1$adj.r.squared, 4)` versus
`r round(email_glance_2$adj.r.squared, 4)`) and the lower AIC
(`r round(email_glance_1$AIC, 2)` versus
`r round(email_glance_2$AIC, 2)`). These statistics account for the additional
complexity. The differences are small, but the extra predictor adds little
useful information. These are in-sample comparisons; they do not demonstrate
better prediction on new observations.

## Exercise 3: Create a workflow to fit a model

```{r split-data}
set.seed(1234)
gss16_split <- initial_split(gss16_advfront)
gss16_train <- training(gss16_split)
gss16_test  <- testing(gss16_split)
```

#### Exercise 3 (a)

```{r workflow-1}
gss16_rec_1 <- recipe(advfront ~ educ, data = gss16_train)

gss16_mod_1 <- logistic_reg() %>%
  set_engine("glm") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

gss16_wflow_1 <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(gss16_rec_1) %>%
  add_model(gss16_mod_1)

gss16_wflow_1
```

I choose **binary logistic regression** because `advfront` has two outcome
categories. It models the log-odds of agreement as a linear function of
education and produces probabilities between zero and one. The `glm`
engine fits a binomial model with a logit link. Education is already numeric,
so no dummy encoding is needed for this first recipe.

The specified split gives `r nrow(gss16_train)` training observations and `r nrow(gss16_test)` test observations. Both logistic models use this same split, with fitting and preprocessing learned only from the training data.

#### Exercise 3 (b)

```{r fit-and-predict-1, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
gss16_fit_1 <- fit(gss16_wflow_1, data = gss16_train)

gss16_pred_1 <- bind_cols(
  gss16_test %>% select(advfront),
  predict(gss16_fit_1, new_data = gss16_test, type = "prob")
)

roc_1 <- roc_curve(gss16_pred_1, truth = advfront, .pred_Agree,
                   event_level = "second")
auc_1 <- roc_auc(gss16_pred_1, truth = advfront, .pred_Agree,
                 event_level = "second")

autoplot(roc_1) +
  labs(title = "Model 1: education only",
       subtitle = paste("Test ROC AUC =", round(auc_1$.estimate, 3)),
       x = "False positive rate (1 - specificity)",
       y = "True positive rate (sensitivity)")
```

"Agree" is the positive event throughout. Because it is the **second**
factor level, `event_level = "second"` must be used with `.pred_Agree` in
the ROC and performance calculations (see the
[yardstick documentation](https://yardstick.tidymodels.org/reference/roc_auc.html)).
The ROC curve shows sensitivity against the false positive rate across
thresholds. The test AUC is **`r round(auc_1$.estimate, 3)`**;
0.5 represents chance-level ranking and 1 represents perfect ranking.

## Exercise 4: Performance of a logistic regression

#### Exercise 4 (a)

```{r confusion-matrix-083}
gss16_pred_1 <- gss16_pred_1 %>%
  mutate(
    .pred_class = factor(
      if_else(.pred_Agree >= 0.83, "Agree", "Not agree"),
      levels = levels(gss16_test$advfront)
    )
  )

conf_mat(gss16_pred_1, truth = advfront, estimate = .pred_class)

counts_083 <- gss16_pred_1 %>%
  summarise(
    TP = sum(advfront == "Agree" & .pred_class == "Agree"),
    TN = sum(advfront == "Not agree" & .pred_class == "Not agree"),
    FP = sum(advfront == "Not agree" & .pred_class == "Agree"),
    FN = sum(advfront == "Agree" & .pred_class == "Not agree")
  )

counts_083 %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Outcome", values_to = "Count") %>%
  mutate(Meaning = c("True positive", "True negative",
                     "False positive", "False negative")) %>%
  select(Outcome, Meaning, Count) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Test predictions at the 0.83 cutoff; positive = Agree")

metrics_083 <- bind_rows(
  sens(gss16_pred_1, truth = advfront, estimate = .pred_class,
       event_level = "second"),
  spec(gss16_pred_1, truth = advfront, estimate = .pred_class,
       event_level = "second")
)
knitr::kable(metrics_083, digits = 4,
             caption = "Sensitivity and specificity at the 0.83 cutoff")
```

The cutoff is applied to the **unrounded** probability of agreement, with
equality included in the "Agree" prediction. The resulting rates are

\[
\text{Sensitivity} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}
= \frac{`r counts_083$TP`}{`r counts_083$TP` + `r counts_083$FN`}
= `r round(counts_083$TP / (counts_083$TP + counts_083$FN), 4)`,
\]

\[
\text{Specificity} = \frac{TN}{TN+FP}
= \frac{`r counts_083$TN`}{`r counts_083$TN` + `r counts_083$FP`}
= `r round(counts_083$TN / (counts_083$TN + counts_083$FP), 4)`.
\]

The model correctly identifies
`r round(100 * counts_083$TP / (counts_083$TP + counts_083$FN), 1)`%
of respondents who agree and
`r round(100 * counts_083$TN / (counts_083$TN + counts_083$FP), 1)`%
of respondents who do not agree. Sensitivity and specificity measure
performance within the actual positive and negative groups, respectively;
they are not the overall accuracy.

#### Exercise 4 (b)

```{r workflow-2}
gss16_rec_2 <- recipe(
  advfront ~ polviews + wrkstat + emailhr + educ,
  data = gss16_train
) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal(), -all_outcomes())

gss16_mod_2 <- logistic_reg() %>%
  set_engine("glm") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

gss16_wflow_2 <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(gss16_rec_2) %>%
  add_model(gss16_mod_2)

gss16_fit_2 <- fit(gss16_wflow_2, data = gss16_train)

gss16_pred_2 <- bind_cols(
  gss16_test %>% select(advfront),
  predict(gss16_fit_2, new_data = gss16_test, type = "prob")
)

roc_2 <- roc_curve(gss16_pred_2, truth = advfront, .pred_Agree,
                   event_level = "second")
auc_2 <- roc_auc(gss16_pred_2, truth = advfront, .pred_Agree,
                 event_level = "second")

auc_comparison <- bind_rows(
  "Model 1: educ" = auc_1,
  "Model 2: polviews + wrkstat + emailhr + educ" = auc_2,
  .id = "Model"
)
knitr::kable(auc_comparison, digits = 4, caption = "Test ROC AUC comparison")
```

The second model is also logistic regression because the outcome is still
binary. `step_dummy(all_nominal(), -all_outcomes())` encodes the categorical
predictors and explicitly excludes `advfront`. By default, it creates one
fewer dummy variable than the number of levels for each predictor (see the
[recipes documentation](https://recipes.tidymodels.org/reference/step_dummy.html)).
The workflow learns this encoding on the training data and applies it to
the test data.

```{r compare-roc, fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.cap="ROC curves evaluated on the same held-out test observations."}
bind_rows("Model 1: educ" = roc_1,
          "Model 2: all four predictors" = roc_2,
          .id = "Model") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = 1 - specificity, y = sensitivity, colour = Model)) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed",
              colour = "grey55") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#28536B", "#C05A32")) +
  labs(x = "False positive rate (1 - specificity)",
       y = "True positive rate (sensitivity)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**`r if (auc_2$.estimate > auc_1$.estimate) "Model 2" else "Model 1"`
performs better on this test set according to ROC AUC.** Model 1 has AUC
`r round(auc_1$.estimate, 4)` and Model 2 has AUC
`r round(auc_2$.estimate, 4)`, an absolute difference of
`r round(abs(auc_2$.estimate - auc_1$.estimate), 4)`.
Higher AUC indicates better ranking of respondents who agree above those
who do not agree across thresholds; it is not the percentage correctly
classified at a particular cutoff. Adding predictors does not guarantee
better performance on unseen observations.

Both AUC values are close to 0.5, so neither model discriminates well between
the two groups. In this split, the additional predictors do not improve
out-of-sample ranking; the simpler model is preferable by the chosen metric.

This comparison uses the same held-out observations for both models, but
it is based on one random split. It does not establish a statistically
significant difference or guarantee the same ranking in other samples.
ROC AUC also does not assess probability calibration or the practical
costs of false positives and false negatives.
